## Summary

After 1918, Austria was a small country left with the capital of a large empire, cut off from the farmland and coal it used to rely on, and it ran its budget on the printing press. Inflation passed 50 % a month from October 1921. It peaked in **August 1922 at 129 % in the month, with prices doubling every 25.5 days** (H&K). By then, consumer prices were **14,000 times** their pre-war level. A League of Nations loan in October 1922, conditional on budget control, stopped it within weeks.

## Causes

- **The empire broke apart.** Each successor state stamped or replaced the common Austro-Hungarian
  notes; Austria stamped its own "Deutschösterreich" on 12 March 1919.
- **A state that could not pay for itself.** Food subsidies, a large civil service sized for the
  empire, and war debts, all paid with new money: the money supply grew more than tenfold between
  1920 and 1921.

## Timeline

- **12 Mar 1919** — the notes are stamped "Deutschösterreich".
- **1920–1921** — the money supply goes from 12 billion to about 147 billion kronen.
- **Oct 1921** — monthly inflation passes 50 % (H&K start).
- **Aug 1922** — the peak: 129 % (H&K). Prices are 14,000 times their pre-war level.
- **4 Oct 1922** — the Geneva Protocols are signed. The League of Nations lends 650 million gold kronen, a League commissioner controls the budget, and an independent central bank is created.
- **20 Dec 1924** — the schilling is adopted (10,000 K = 1 S) and enters circulation in 1925.

## The end

Stopping the inflation needed two things at once: an **outside lender** that controlled the budget, and a **central bank that was no longer allowed to finance the state**. The krone stopped falling **as soon as the loan was announced**, before any money arrived, because expectations turned.

## Lessons

- The quickest case in the set: credibility came from an outside commitment, so the currency
  stabilised before the reform itself took effect.
- It is a template for the "anchor + ban + fiscal fix" pattern (see , pattern 5).
